evidence_set: Heroin: the letter says that higher heroin availability until 2001, which declined by 2002 and stayed low, was tracked in two earlier papers by three of the study's authors (references 3 and 4); in the later one (Kerr et al., 2007, as cited), 21% of a large Vancouver cohort reported a non-fatal overdose in the previous 12 months in 1997, 12% at the beginning of 2001, 5% by the end of 2001 and 6% in 2004, which, it says, those authors put down to reduced heroin supply; it sets this against the study's statement that the authors had no evidence of significant changes in drug supply or purity during the study period, 2001 to 2005. Policing: it says that three of the study's authors wrote a 2004 paper on the displacement of people who use drugs out of the policed area around Insite in 2003 and into other areas of Vancouver (reference 5), recording counts of discarded needles 46% lower in the policed areas and higher by similar proportions elsewhere in the city, against the study's statement that the authors knew of no changes in policing policy that could have confounded the results; that most of the deaths behind the 35% reduction lay in the 12 city blocks patrolled by 48–66 police added in 2003 and still deployed (a personal communication, the source not named); and that this change in policing is clearly the most likely cause of any real reduction near the facility. No deaths in the policed blocks are counted; the non-fatal overdose and needle figures are second-hand. Editors' note: both statements of the study are worded so in it (Marshall et al., 2011, p. 1434 on supply, p. 1435 on policing). The letter's reference 3, dated 2004 there, has the same authors, title, volume (101) and pages (689–95) as the study's own reference 44 (p. 1437), dated 2006, which the study cites on p. 1434 for drug-use patterns that stayed largely constant from 2001 to 2005 (daily heroin injecting 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005; anchor 5): the two sides draw on the same paper, the letter for a fall in heroin supply and the study for stable drug use. That paper (Wood et al., 2006) has since been read from its PDF (anchors 19 to 22): it dates from 2006, as the study has it; its data end in 2003 (December 2004 for its cohort), and it contains neither of the study's figures.

The authors note a decline over time in the proportion of participants reporting a non-fatal overdose, the most substantial during 2001, and write that it is consistent with other reports of a reduction in heroin-related overdoses during this period (Wood et al., 2006, as cited) and suggests that global reductions in heroin supply may have played a role; it may also be related to the protective effect of methadone treatment and the significant expansion of methadone treatment availability in British Columbia from 1995 to 2004 (Anderson and Warren, 2004, as cited). They also note that a supervised injection facility had recently opened in Vancouver and that its impact on overdose had not yet been evaluated. Limitations: VIDUS is not a random sample, so the findings may not generalize to other populations of people who inject drugs; overdoses were self-defined by participants asked whether they had had an overdose in the past 6 months, an approach the authors say may introduce an element of subjectivity but offers advantages where polysubstance use is the norm, adding that the definitions used in previous studies also introduce limitations related to recall bias and do not provide a hard diagnosis of overdose; the exact temporal relationship between the outcome and the explanatory variables could not be ascertained, so the study does not allow a thorough investigation of causal relationships; and although it has been suggested that changing drug purity may play a role in predicting overdose (Darke et al., 1999, as cited), the authors were unable to consider it. Editors' notes: the study recorded no measure of heroin supply, availability, price or purity, so its explanation of the decline rests on the papers it cites. The letter (anchor 9) says these authors clearly point to reduced heroin supply as the reason; the paper says reduced supply may have played a role and adds methadone expansion as a possible reason. The paper it cites for the reduction in heroin-related overdoses (Wood et al., 2006, volume 101, pages 689–95, on Canadian heroin supply) is the letter's reference 3, dated 2004 there, and the study's own reference 44 (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 1434, 1437); read since from its PDF (anchors 19 to 22), it reports fewer overdose deaths across British Columbia and fewer naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in the Downtown Eastside in 2001–03 than in 1998–2000, and measured no heroin purity.

evidence_add.extracted: A paper by five authors, three of them authors of the study (Wood, Montaner and Kerr), on markers of heroin use and harm in western Canada before and after the Australian heroin shortage, which it dates from about January 2001. Its stated primary hypothesis was that the markers would stay stable or rise, because western Canada receives heroin from similar source countries and, citing one paper, had not changed its supply-reduction funding or activities since the mid-1990s. It compared yearly averages, with no statistical test and no comparison series, of overdose deaths in the whole province of British Columbia from the provincial vital statistics registry, 1998–2000 against 2001–03 (the drugs responsible were not available, and some deaths would probably not involve heroin); ambulance responses that required naloxone in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside, fiscal years 1997–98 to 2000–01 against 2001–02 to 2002–03; and the weight of heroin destined for Canada that was seized, 1998–2000 against 2001–03, a potential indicator of supply that, the authors note, could also mark supply-reduction activity. In VIDUS, a prospective cohort of people who inject drugs in Vancouver interviewed every 6 months, daily heroin use reported from May 1996 to December 2004 was compared between 1996–2000 and 2001–04 by GEE logistic regression, with potential confounders including methadone use and residence in the Downtown Eastside. Editors' note: the death series is titled drug-induced deaths in its source (reference 19, p. 694); no series measures heroin purity, price or availability directly, none covers an area smaller than the Downtown Eastside, and none goes beyond 2003 (December 2004 for the cohort); the paper does not mention supervised injection.

evidence_add.extracted: Yearly averages (Table 1): 297 overdose deaths in British Columbia in 1998–2000 against 192 in 2001–03 (35.4% reduction); 674 naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in the Downtown Eastside a year in fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01 against 370 in 2001–02 to 2002–03 (45.1%); 184 kg of heroin destined for Canada seized a year against 67 kg (63.6%); no intervals or statistical tests. Figure 1 plots the yearly values without printing them. Editors' reading of Figure 1 at 300 dpi (approximate; bar tops read inside the bar outlines against the axis ticks, and checked against the bar rectangles drawn in the PDF): deaths about 399 (1998), 272 (1999), 218 (2000), 221 (2001), 169 (2002) and 186 (2003); naloxone-requiring responses about 732, 840, 655, 464, 388 and 350 (fiscal 1997–98 to 2002–03); heroin seized about 234, 142, 177, 94, 46 and 60 kg (1998 to 2003). The means of these readings by period (296 and 192 deaths, 673 and 369 responses, 184 and 67 kg) are each within 1 of Table 1. Editors' calculations from the readings: deaths fell about 45% from 1998 to 2000, about four-fifths of their fall to the lowest year (2002), were about the same in 2001 as in 2000, and were about 52 and 35 lower in 2002 and 2003 than in 2001; naloxone-requiring responses peaked in fiscal 1998–99 and fell in every later year, with 2000–01 already about 45% below the peak; seizures fell from 1998 to 1999, rose in 2000, and were lower in every year from 2001 than in any earlier year (2001 about half of 2000 and twice 2002). The paper does not comment on the falls before 2001. Its text gives the seizure period as 2000–03 where Table 1 and the abstract give 2001–03, a misprint (the readings for 2001–03 average about 67 kg).

evidence_add.extracted: In VIDUS, 1587 participants provided 13 609 data points at which daily heroin use could be assessed between May 1996 and December 2004. Adjusted for daily cocaine injection, daily crack use, sex-trade involvement, current methadone use, age, Downtown Eastside residence, Aboriginal ethnicity and gender, daily heroin injection was less likely in 2001–04 than in 1996–2000 (adjusted odds ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.50–0.61, P<0.001). Broken down into two-year periods, the proportion reporting daily use was 36.5% in 1997/98, 32.6% in 1999/00, 23.3% in 2001/02 and 20.8% in 2003/04, with no counts or denominators; other drugs did not fall similarly, and methamphetamine use rose significantly (data not shown). Editors' note: self-reported, in one cohort, and not split by area; 2001 is not shown apart from 2002, and nothing is given for 2005. The study cites this paper (its reference 44; Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 1434, 1437) for drug-use patterns that stayed largely constant from 2001 to 2005, with daily heroin injecting of 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005, daily cocaine injecting of 17% and 15%, and stable methadone and other treatment use (anchor 5). None of these figures is in this paper, whose cohort data end in December 2004, show daily heroin injection lower after 2000 (and 2.5 percentage points lower in 2003/04 than in 2001/02, editors' calculation), and include no yearly figures for daily cocaine injection or methadone use. The authors' reply cites a different 2006 paper by the same five authors (same journal, volume 101, pages 623–625) and a 2009 web report for stable daily heroin use (anchor 12); neither is on file.

evidence_add.extracted: The authors conclude that massive decreases in markers of heroin use were seen in western Canada coinciding with the Australian heroin shortage, despite no increases in funding to Canadian enforcement efforts, and that external global heroin supply forces deserve greater investigation and credence as an explanation of the Australian shortage; they acknowledge that supply may instead have been diverted elsewhere, or production switched to other drugs such as methamphetamine. Limitations they state: overdose statistics and seizure data may be poor proxies for heroin use; the measures were not counted at the same level, and fiscal years put 4 months of post-shortage data in the period before the shortage for naloxone; Canada has no standardized longitudinal measures of street heroin purity, although other studies (cited) found ambulance visits and overdose mortality statistics to correlate strongly with street purity. Funding: the cohort is supported by the US National Institutes of Health and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research; the article has no conflict-of-interest statement. Editors' note: the paper's evidence for unchanged Canadian enforcement is one citation, with no data shown; its statement that reduced heroin availability on Vancouver's streets was widely reported in the media cites a paper on HIV treatment (its reference 17); it measured neither heroin purity nor price.
